before.title: ECM Relay Engine Stalling (Recall 10V517000)
before.description: The IPDM (Intelligent Power Distribution Module) contains an ECM relay with a noise-reduction diode. Over time silicon evaporates from the diode molding and silicon oxide builds up on the relay contacts due to arcing, which can interrupt power to the engine control module and cause the engine to stall, especially at low speeds. NHTSA recall 10V517000 covers roughly 747,000 Nissan vehicles including 2005-2006 Xterra.
before.solution: Under recall 10V517000, dealers replace the ECM relay inside the IPDM assembly free of charge regardless of whether it has failed yet. Owners should verify recall completion by VIN; the relay can also be replaced as an inexpensive standalone part if symptoms occur on out-of-recall vehicles.
symptoms: Engine stalls unexpectedly, often at low speed or idle
Intermittent no-start or hard-start
Stalling that worsens over time
Loss of engine power while driving

before.title: First-Generation Exhaust Manifold Cracking (3.3L V6)
before.description: First-generation (2000-2004) Xterras with the 3.3L VG33E/VG33ER V6 commonly crack the passenger-side (right) exhaust manifold over time due to heat cycling. A Nissan TSB acknowledged the issue. A cracked manifold produces a ticking/exhaust leak noise that is loudest on cold start, can trigger the check-engine light, and can affect downstream oxygen-sensor readings and performance.
before.solution: Replace the cracked exhaust manifold (welding repairs typically fail and re-crack, so owners are advised to replace with a new or upgraded manifold). Replace manifold gaskets and any seized exhaust studs at the same time. Inspect both manifolds since the right side is most prone but either can crack.
symptoms: Ticking or tapping exhaust-leak noise, loudest on cold start
Noise that quiets as the engine warms up
Exhaust smell
Reduced performance / fuel economy
Check engine light from skewed O2 sensor readings

before.title: First-Generation Head Gasket Failure (3.3L V6)
before.description: The first-generation 3.3L V6 is prone to head gasket failure, aggravated by heat soak at the rear cylinders (5 and 6) near the firewall where the catalytic-converter heat builds up and can make rear injectors fail and those cylinders run hotter. Failures typically appear at higher mileage and result in coolant/oil mixing or coolant loss and overheating.
before.solution: Replace the head gaskets (often both sides) and resurface/inspect the heads; verify cylinder heads are not warped or cracked. Address cooling-system condition and any failing rear fuel injectors at the same time. Catching coolant loss early and not driving while overheating prevents head/block damage.
symptoms: Coolant mixed into the oil (milky residue on dipstick/oil cap)
Overheating
White exhaust smoke / sweet coolant smell
Coolant loss without obvious external leak
Combustion gases / exhaust bubbling from the radiator with cap off

before.title: Front Lower Ball Joint / Control Arm Wear
before.description: The front lower control arms on second-generation Xterras integrate the lower ball joints, which wear out and develop play, producing clunking over bumps and wandering, loose steering. Worn ball joints also throw off alignment and cause premature inner/outer front tire wear. Because the ball joint is part of the control arm, the typical repair is the full lower control arm assembly.
before.solution: Inspect front lower ball joints for play during service; replace the worn lower control arm assembly (which includes the ball joint and bushings) and perform a four-wheel alignment afterward. Replacing in pairs is common. Note a 2009-2010 service-part recall (10V517000-era aftermarket control-arm campaign 10V517 is separate; replacement control arms recall was 10V517000/10V517—verify part recall 10V517000 vs the lower control arm campaign by VIN).
symptoms: Clunking or knocking from the front end over bumps
Wandering or loose-feeling steering
Uneven / premature front tire wear
Vibration or play felt in the steering

before.title: Radiator-to-Transmission Coolant Cross-Contamination ("Strawberry Milkshake of Death" / SMOD)
before.description: The factory Calsonic radiator on second-generation (N50) Xterras with the VQ40DE V6 and automatic transmission has an internal transmission-fluid cooler whose seal fails over time, allowing engine coolant and ATF to mix. The resulting pink, milkshake-like sludge circulates into the transmission, destroying valve-body solenoids, clutches and seals and often the transmission entirely. This is the single most notorious and catastrophic Xterra defect, prompting a class-action lawsuit and a Nissan warranty extension. Once contamination occurs the transmission is usually beyond saving and a coolant flush alone will not fix it.
before.solution: Inspect coolant and ATF regularly for any pink/brown frothy contamination. The permanent prevention is a 'radiator bypass': disconnect the transmission cooler circuit from the factory radiator and route ATF through a dedicated external air-to-oil cooler, then install an aftermarket all-metal or bypassed radiator. If contamination has already occurred, the transmission must be replaced/rebuilt and the entire cooling and trans circuit flushed; affected owners should check eligibility under the Nissan radiator class-action settlement and the 8yr/80k-mile warranty extension.
symptoms: Pink or brown frothy 'milkshake' sludge in the radiator or coolant reservoir
Contaminated (foamy/pink) transmission fluid on the dipstick
Harsh, erratic, or delayed shifting
Transmission slipping or going into limp/fail-safe mode
Engine overheating
Complete transmission failure

before.title: Secondary Timing Chain / Tensioner Guide Noise (VQ40DE)
before.description: Early second-generation Xterras with the VQ40DE V6 suffer from a buzzing/whining noise from the timing chain area that rises in pitch with engine RPM. The Borg-Warner secondary timing chains had links stamped with worn tooling, leaving sharp edges that cut through the plastic tensioner shoes and guides. Nissan issued TSB NTB07-042 covering the redesigned chains and tensioner shoes. If left unaddressed, the chain can wear into the metal plunger, eventually risking timing problems and engine damage.
before.solution: Per TSB NTB07-042, replace both secondary timing chains and both secondary tensioner shoes with the redesigned parts (chains P/N 13028ZK00B; tensioners 13070-ZK01A / 13070-ZK01B). Many shops also inspect/replace the primary chain, guides, and water pump while the front of the engine is open. Address the noise early before the chain wears into metal.
symptoms: High-frequency buzzing or whining noise from the front of the engine
Noise increases in frequency/pitch with engine RPM
Most noticeable at idle and low RPM when cold
Possible rattle on startup in worse cases

before.title: Timing Chain Guide Failure (VQ40DE Engine)
before.description: The Xterra VQ40DE 4.0L V6 shares the same timing chain guide failure as the Frontier. The plastic guides deteriorate and shatter, causing chain rattle and potential catastrophic engine damage. This issue typically occurs between 80,000-130,000 miles and is the second most common Xterra problem after SMOD.
before.solution: Replace all timing chain guides, tensioners, and chains. Use updated Nissan parts or Cloyes aftermarket kit. Labor-intensive repair requiring 8-12 hours. Cost: $1,500-3,000. Address immediately upon hearing any chain rattle.
symptoms: Rattling noise on cold start
Chain rattle at idle
Check engine light with timing codes
Metal debris in oil
Engine running rough
